title: The baptism (Matthew 3:13–17)
hook: Jesus goes under the Jordan, and a voice says: this is my beloved son

segments.voice: Yesterday, metanoia: John by the river, calling crowds to change their minds and turn around.

Some words can't be earned. Nobody is called beloved because of a good report card. At the Jordan, John is baptizing crowds, people turning around and starting again. One day a man from Nazareth, about thirty years old, joins the line. He hasn't preached a sermon. He hasn't healed anyone. As far as anyone knows, he's a builder from a small town in Galilee. And John looks at him and stops.
screen: `SOME WORDS CAN'T BE EARNED.` → `A MAN FROM NAZARETH JOINS THE LINE.` → `JOHN STOPS.`

segments.voice: Baptism comes from the Greek baptizo: to dip, to plunge, to immerse, an ordinary Greek word for putting something under. John tries to refuse: "I have need to be baptized of thee, and comest thou to me?" Jesus answers: "Suffer it to be so now: for thus it becometh us to fulfil all righteousness." Suffer here means allow. So he goes down into the water, like everyone else in the line. Readers have asked ever since why he would stand with people turning from their wrongs. One old answer: he chose to stand exactly where they stood. He comes up out of the water, and "the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him." And a voice from heaven: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Look at the timing. No miracles yet, no teaching, no followers. Beloved first; the work comes after. Christians who confess the Trinity see it here: the Father's voice, the Son in the water, the Spirit like a dove, in one scene. Catholics and others in the West keep a feast of the Baptism of the Lord. Orthodox Christians call it Theophany, God shown, and bless water. Baptism became the door into the church, though churches do it differently. Catholics, Orthodox, Lutherans and Anglicans baptize babies. Baptists and others baptize those old enough to profess faith. Some pour, some sprinkle, some go all the way under. The words said over the water come from the end of Matthew's Gospel: in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.
screen: `BAPTIZO: TO DIP, TO PLUNGE.` · `HE STANDS IN LINE WITH EVERYONE.` · `A DOVE AND A VOICE.` · `ONE WATER, MANY WAYS.` · then, large: `THIS IS MY BELOVED SON.`

segments.voice: If you can, hold your hands under warm running water at a sink and feel it run slowly over your fingers and palms; if you can't get to water, rest your hands open in your lap and imagine it. While it runs, notice that you haven't done anything to earn this moment; you're just here. If you pray, hear the word beloved as spoken to you; if not, let the water be water.
Baptism. From the Greek for dip or plunge. Washing with water as a door into a new life, and the scene where Jesus is called beloved before he does a thing.
Your line: beloved, before anything else. Tomorrow that word gets tested. See you in the desert.

screen: `DAY 48 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: FORTY DAYS IN THE WILDERNESS.`

howItsDone: Christians are baptized with water, usually in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit: as infants in Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Anglican churches, and as believers in Baptist and many other churches. Many churches keep the Baptism of the Lord in January, and Orthodox Christians bless water at Theophany.

notes: 'Builder': Mark 6:3 and Matthew 13:55 use tekton (craftsman, builder, often translated carpenter). Confirm the word choice.
The question why the sinless Jesus is baptized is answered with one common reading (solidarity with sinners); other readings exist (fulfilling righteousness, consecrating the waters).
Infant vs believer's baptism and modes (immersion, pouring, sprinkling) summarized; Orthodox baptize by triple immersion, including infants. Confirm the church lists.
'Nearly all use water and the triune name' — some groups (e.g., Oneness Pentecostals, Quakers, The Salvation Army) differ; kept as 'nearly all'.
Feast of the Baptism of the Lord (Catholic, Sunday after Epiphany); Orthodox Theophany, January 6, with the Great Blessing of Waters.
